items.correct: an exothermic reaction occurring continuously in living cells
items.misconception: an endothermic reaction happening in all living cells
items.why: Students see that glucose and oxygen are taken into the cell and assume energy must be taken in as well, and 'exothermic' and 'endothermic' are easily swapped. Cellular respiration is an exothermic reaction, which is why organisms can use the energy transferred for keeping warm.
items.random_wrong: an exothermic reaction happening during exercise

items.q: How does anaerobic respiration in muscle cells compare with aerobic respiration?
items.correct: less energy transferred, and lactic acid made
items.misconception: far more energy transferred, and lactic acid made
items.why: Anaerobic respiration is associated with sudden bursts of intense activity, so students confuse the rate of the reaction with the amount of energy transferred per glucose molecule. As the oxidation of glucose is incomplete in anaerobic respiration, much less energy is transferred than in aerobic respiration.
items.random_wrong: less energy transferred, and ethanol also made

items.q: Which is a use of the energy transferred by respiration?
items.correct: building larger molecules from smaller ones
items.misconception: creating new energy inside the cell
items.why: Phrases such as 'releases energy' and 'produces energy' are common in everyday language, so energy is treated as a substance that can be made and destroyed. Energy is transferred, not made. The energy transferred by respiration supplies all the energy needed for living processes such as building larger molecules, movement and keeping warm.
items.random_wrong: moving oxygen out of the lungs and into the blood

items.q: Which word equation represents aerobic respiration?
items.why: The aerobic equation is learned first and students apply its products to every kind of respiration, especially as people do breathe out carbon dioxide during exercise. Anaerobic respiration in muscles is represented by the equation glucose → lactic acid. The oxidation of glucose is incomplete, so carbon dioxide and water are not the products.

items.q: In the equation for aerobic respiration, what do the symbols C6H12O6 and H2O represent?
items.correct: C6H12O6 is glucose and H2O is the water produced
items.misconception: C6H12O6 is glucose and H2O is oxygen
items.why: Students match symbols by the letters they can see rather than reading the whole formula, and both formulae contain C and O. Students should recognise the chemical symbols: C6H12O6 is glucose, O2 is oxygen, CO2 is carbon dioxide and H2O is water.
items.random_wrong: C6H12O6 is oxygen gas and H2O is water

items.q: A muscle cell has no oxygen supply. Which substance builds up in the cell?
items.why: Lactic acid is met first, in the well known example of muscles during exercise, and is then treated as the product of all anaerobic respiration. Anaerobic respiration in muscles produces lactic acid, but anaerobic respiration in plant and yeast cells produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.

items.q: Why is much less energy transferred by anaerobic respiration than by aerobic respiration?
items.correct: the oxidation of glucose is incomplete
items.misconception: the oxidation of glucose is faster
items.why: Anaerobic respiration is associated with sudden bursts of intense activity, so students confuse the rate of the reaction with the amount of energy transferred per glucose molecule. As the oxidation of glucose is incomplete in anaerobic respiration, much less energy is transferred than in aerobic respiration.
items.random_wrong: the glucose stored in cells is used up faster

items.q: Yeast is used in the manufacture of bread and alcoholic drinks. Which equation represents the respiration of the yeast in these processes?
items.why: Lactic acid is met first, in the well known example of muscles during exercise, and is then treated as the product of all anaerobic respiration. Anaerobic respiration in muscles produces lactic acid, but anaerobic respiration in plant and yeast cells produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.

items.q: How does the body react to the increased demand for energy during exercise?
items.correct: heart rate, breathing rate and breath volume rise
items.misconception: the breathing rate rises but the heart rate stays steady
items.why: Faster breathing is the change students notice in themselves, while breath volume cannot be felt directly and the heart rate is only noticed if it is measured. The heart rate, breathing rate and breath volume increase during exercise to supply the muscles with more oxygenated blood.
items.random_wrong: the breathing rate rises but the breath volume stays the same

items.q: A sprinter's muscles are not supplied with enough oxygen during a race. What happens in the muscles?
items.correct: lactic acid builds up and an oxygen debt forms
items.misconception: carbon dioxide builds up and an oxygen debt forms
items.why: The aerobic equation is learned first and students apply its products to every kind of respiration, especially as people do breathe out carbon dioxide during exercise. Anaerobic respiration in muscles is represented by the equation glucose → lactic acid. The oxidation of glucose is incomplete, so carbon dioxide and water are not the products.
items.random_wrong: ethanol builds up and an oxygen debt is created

items.q: After a race, what happens to the lactic acid that has built up in the muscles?
items.correct: it is taken in the blood to the liver
items.misconception: it is broken down inside the muscles
items.why: Lactic acid builds up in muscles and that is where the aching is felt, so students assume the muscle also removes it and do not connect the process with another organ. Blood flowing through the muscles transports the lactic acid to the liver where it is converted back into glucose. Oxygen debt is the amount of extra oxygen the body needs after exercise to react with the accumulated lactic acid and remove it from the cells.
items.random_wrong: it is breathed out through the lungs as vapour

items.q: How is a lipid molecule formed in metabolism?
items.correct: from one glycerol and three fatty acids
items.misconception: from three glycerols and a fatty acid
items.why: Students remember that the numbers one and three are involved but not which small molecule each number belongs to, and 'glycerol' and 'fatty acid' are unfamiliar names. Metabolism includes the formation of lipid molecules from a molecule of glycerol and three molecules of fatty acids.
items.random_wrong: from a single glycerol and three amino acids

items.q: A plant cell synthesises protein. Which molecules does its metabolism use?
items.correct: glucose and nitrate ions, used to make amino acids
items.misconception: glucose and some fatty acids, to make amino acids
items.why: Glucose is remembered as the starting point for everything a plant makes, and the nitrate ions taken up by the roots are easy to leave out because they are not part of photosynthesis. Metabolism includes the use of glucose and nitrate ions to form amino acids which in turn are used to synthesise proteins.
items.random_wrong: glycerol and nitrate ions, to make amino acids

items.q: Is respiration the same thing as breathing?
items.correct: Respiration is an exothermic reaction occurring continuously in living cells that transfers energy from glucose. Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs, and the breathing rate increases during exercise to supply the muscles with more oxygenated blood.
items.misconception: Respiration is breathing air in and out, so it happens in the lungs rather than in cells.
items.why: In everyday speech 'respiration' and 'respiratory system' are used for breathing, and both processes involve oxygen and carbon dioxide, so students merge the two. Cellular respiration is an exothermic reaction which is continuously occurring in living cells. Breathing supplies the oxygen used in aerobic respiration and removes the carbon dioxide made, but it is not respiration itself.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.correct: Respiration occurs continuously in living cells, whether the organism is resting or exercising.
items.misconception: Cells only respire when the body is exercising and needs extra energy.
items.why: Respiration is usually met through examples about exercise and muscles, so students link it to activity rather than to all living cells all of the time. Cellular respiration is continuously occurring in living cells because the energy transferred supplies all the energy needed for living processes, including at rest.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is the energy transferred by respiration used for in chemical reactions?
items.correct: It is used for chemical reactions to build larger molecules, for example forming starch, glycogen, lipids and proteins.
items.misconception: The energy from respiration is used to break large molecules down into small ones.
items.why: Students associate respiration with the breakdown of glucose and assume that other reactions in the body must also be breakdown reactions. Organisms need energy for chemical reactions to build larger molecules, as well as for movement and keeping warm. Metabolism uses this energy in enzyme controlled processes that synthesise new molecules.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What are the reactants of aerobic respiration?
items.correct: The reactants are glucose and oxygen; the products are carbon dioxide and water.
items.misconception: Aerobic respiration uses carbon dioxide and water to make glucose and oxygen.
items.why: Respiration and photosynthesis are taught as linked processes with the same four substances, so students reverse the equation. Aerobic respiration is represented by the equation glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water, so glucose and oxygen are used up and carbon dioxide and water are produced.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does fermentation in yeast need oxygen?
items.correct: Fermentation is anaerobic respiration in yeast cells, so it takes place without oxygen.
items.misconception: Fermentation still needs a small amount of oxygen, because all living cells need oxygen to respire.
items.why: Students learn that organisms need oxygen to survive and assume no cell can transfer energy without it, so they add oxygen to the fermentation equation. Respiration can take place anaerobically, without oxygen. Anaerobic respiration in yeast cells is called fermentation and is represented by glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide, with no oxygen used.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can any small molecule be used to build any larger molecule?
items.correct: Each larger molecule is built from its own small molecules: sugars build carbohydrates, glycerol and fatty acids build lipids, and amino acids build proteins.
items.misconception: The small molecules are interchangeable, so amino acids, glycerol or sugars can be used to build whichever larger molecule the cell needs.
items.why: The small molecules are all products of digestion that are met together in one list, so students treat them as one general supply of building blocks. Metabolism includes conversion of glucose to starch, glycogen and cellulose; the formation of lipid molecules from a molecule of glycerol and three molecules of fatty acids; and the use of glucose and nitrate ions to form amino acids which in turn are used to synthesise proteins.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented
